name: Hakkaisan Brewery (Hakkaisan Jozo, Minamiuonuma)
text: Sake brewery founded in 1922 (Taisho 11) at Nagamori, Minamiuonuma city, at the foot of Mt Hakkai in snowy Uonuma. Flagship brand is the sake 'Hakkaisan'. Brewing water is the subterranean flow of Mt Hakkai, the spring called 'Raiden-sama no shimizu'. Production is split between two kura, the Kowa-gura and the Dai-ni Kowa-gura.
flavor: Hakkaisan is widely described as the clean, dry (tanrei-karakuchi) style typical of Niigata.
use: Served as a table sake in Niigata cuisine and sold nationally; the company's own site and the prefectural tourism page are the references for visiting.
craft: Sources name the water (Mt Hakkai subterranean flow, 'Raiden-sama no shimizu') as the identity of the house. Sources disagree on who currently represents the company (a news-style source names Nagumo Masahito, the company overview lists Nagumo Jiro as representative director), so check the company page before quoting a name.

name: Asahi Shuzo (Kubota, Nagaoka)
text: Sake brewery in Nagaoka, Niigata, counted among the oldest in the prefecture; one source gives Tenpo 1 (1830) as its founding year while another only says 'Edo period', so the year is not uniform across sources. Its flagship brand 'Kubota' takes its name from the house name (yago) used at founding. Brewing water is soft groundwater from the water vein running through the Asahi district.
flavor: Kubota is associated with the clean, soft-water Niigata style.
use: Brand name sake sold nationally; a standard reference for Niigata's tanrei style when comparing regions.
craft: The soft groundwater (low hardness) is the quoted basis of the house style; as the founding year varies by source, verify with the company before printing it.
src: Hobbytimes: Niigata sake, Kubota and Hakkaisan

name: Ishimoto Shuzo (Koshi no Kanbai, Niigata city)
text: Sake brewery in Niigata city whose flagship brand is 'Koshi no Kanbai'. It is described in the sources seen as the brand that ignited the tanrei-karakuchi (light, dry) boom of Japanese sake. Founding year and brewing details were not given in the results seen.
flavor: Light, dry, clean (tanrei-karakuchi) in the way the style is described.
use: A reference brand when explaining the history of Niigata's light-dry style to guests.
craft: Only the brand's historical role is supported by the sources; process, rice and polishing data were not in the results and are deliberately left out.

name: Shibanuma Shoyu (Tsuchiura, 'Otokiwa')
text: Soy sauce house in Tsuchiura, Ibaraki, founded in 1688 (Genroku 1). Edo-period main house and shoyu kura survive, and a Meiji-era moromi kura is open to visitors. Its 'Otokiwa' (お常陸), brewed with Ibaraki soybeans and wheat and matured about a year in traditional wooden barrels, was the first Ibaraki product to win the Minister of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries prize at the Excellent Furusato Food central contest (FY2011).
flavor: Wooden-barrel koikuchi with about a year of maturation.
use: Table and cooking koikuchi from Ibaraki-grown soy and wheat; the visitor-accessible kura is a place to see barrel brewing.
craft: Check the claims that matter to a kitchen: prefectural soy and wheat, wooden barrels, roughly one year of moromi maturation.

name: Numaya Honten (Yatabe, Tsukuba)
text: Founded 1870 in Yatabe, Tsukuba city, Ibaraki. Makes handmade, naturally brewed (tennen jozo) shoyu and additive-free miso, still using the wooden barrels used by generations of the family. Kura tours are taken by reservation.
flavor: Natural-fermentation shoyu and additive-free miso from old barrels.
use: Shoyu and miso for cooking; the kura visit lets cooks see barrel brewing at small scale.
craft: Distinguishing points per its own site: tennen jozo, family-inherited wooden barrels, no additives in miso.

name: Aritaya (Annaka naturally brewed shoyu)
text: Shoyu and miso maker in Annaka, Joshu (Gunma), founded in Tenpo 3 (1832). The house insists on the old method of natural brewing (tennen jozo) for its shoyu and also makes miso.
flavor: Natural-brewed shoyu in the old style.
use: Cooking and table shoyu; one of the few Gunma shoyu houses promoted for natural brewing.
craft: Its identifying claim is natural brewing with no forced warming; other process details (barrel type, duration) were not given in the results seen.

name: Miya Shoyu (Tamasa Shoyu, Futtsu)
text: Shoyu house in Futtsu, southern Chiba, founded 1834. It keeps natural brewing and wooden-barrel preparation and is reported as the only remaining kuramoto in southern Chiba, supporting the koikuchi food culture of Sanuki (佐貫).
use: Cooking shoyu for the Bosoh area; interest for chefs is a small maker using barrels and natural brewing.
craft: Per the source: natural brewing and wooden barrels. Chiba had over 400 shoyu houses in early Showa and only about 13 still brew their own, so a surviving small kura is notable.
src: Resol no Mori: southern Chiba's only kuramoto

name: Yamasa Shoyu (Choshi)
text: Large shoyu maker in Choshi, Chiba, dated to 1645. Its origin is told as Hamaguchi Gihei bringing shoyu-making technique from Yuasa in Wakayama to Choshi. Chiba is Japan's top shoyu-producing prefecture, and factory tours are promoted by the prefecture's tourism site.
flavor: Standard koikuchi of the Choshi tradition.
use: Industrial-scale supplier and public factory tours teaching fermentation.
craft: Link between Yuasa (Wakayama) and Choshi technique is the key historical point; sources dated the firm to 1645 as told in the Chiba tourism page.
src: Chiba Kanko Navi: Yamasa factory tour

name: Kubota Shuzo (Noda, hon-mirin)
text: Described as the only old sake brewery of Noda city, founded in 1872, making hon-mirin by the traditional 'old-style' method associated with Nagareyama. Chiba leads Japan in mirin output; Noda is the shoyu town where in 1917 eight families merged into Noda Shoyu Co., the forerunner of Kikkoman.
flavor: Hon-mirin, sweet and rounded; white mirin cuisine is promoted in Nagareyama.
use: Cooking mirin; compare the old method against industrial mirin for glazes and sauces.
craft: The source's text mixes Noda and Nagareyama, so confirm the exact location and process with the maker before quoting.
src: Resol no Mori: white mirin of Nagareyama

name: Kubota Miso Shoyu (Noda)
text: Shoyu and miso house in Noda, Chiba, describing itself as having more than 80 years of history. It belongs to the Noda brewing district, the area that produced Kikkoman's predecessor Noda Shoyu in 1917. Only the maker's own site was seen for this entry.
use: Local shoyu and miso for cooking.
craft: Founding year and barrel details are not given in the results seen, so only the 80-plus-years claim is made.

name: Terada Honke (Kanzaki, shizen-shu)
text: Sake brewery in Kanzaki town, Katori district, Chiba, which counts 350 years (its own anniversary page), starting from a move from Omi to Kanzaki in the Empo era (1673-81); one retailer gives 1657, so the date is not uniform. Since the 1980s it makes 'shizen-shu': pesticide-free rice only, no additives, fermented by resident kura microbes. Representative brand 'Gonin Musume'. The brewery buildings are nationally registered tangible cultural properties.
flavor: Natural sake from resident-microbe fermentation (sources give no tasting detail).
use: Natural sake for pairing with fermented and vegetable food; the kura also runs a cafe.
craft: Check: organic rice, no additives, kura-resident microbes rather than commercial cultures.

name: Hayashi Shuzoba (Asahi town, Toyama)
text: Toyama's oldest sake brewery, founded in Kanei 3 (1626), at Asahi town on the border with Niigata. The kura is backed by mountains connected to the Northern Alps, with the Hisui coast of the Sea of Japan in front. It draws on abundant water from Japan's major mountain range.
flavor: Water-driven Toyama sake from mountain meltwater.
use: Local sake for Toyama cuisine; the long history is a selling point for traditional pairing.
craft: Per MAFF Hokuriku's export brochure: the oldest in the prefecture; details of process not given in the results.

name: Takasawa Shuzo (Himi)
text: Sake brewery in Himi, Toyama, begun in Meiji 5 (1872), when the sea reached almost to the back of the kura. It is the only Toyama brewery pressing all of its sake in a funa-style tank (zenryo fune-shibori), and it lets sea breeze in to cool steamed rice.
flavor: Toyama Bay coastal sake, fully tank-pressed.
use: Local sake that pairs with Himi seafood.
craft: Distinguishing points are 100 percent tank pressing (fune) and cooling steamed rice with sea air, per the Info Toyama article.

name: Kokuhare Shuzo (Kurobe, Ikuji)
text: Sake brewery in Kurobe, Toyama, founded Meiji 20 (1887). It has brewed ever since with water from 'Iwase-ke no Shimizu', one of the Ikuji district's spring waters.
use: Local sake from the Kurobe alluvial-fan spring area.
craft: The named spring is the defining detail in the results seen.

name: Ginban Shuzo (Kurobe)
text: Sake brewery in Toyama founded 1910, using spring water from the Kurobe River alluvial fan (Kurobegawa senjochi yusuigun) for brewing.
flavor: Spring-water sake from the Kurobe fan.
use: Regional sake of Toyama.
craft: Water source is the point stressed by the sources; no further detail was found.

name: Okubo Jozoten (Kanro shoyu, Toyama)
text: Toyama shoyu house known for 'Kanro Shoyu'. It puts weight on thinking through the best environment for the microorganisms. Only a short mention was found; founding year and process figures were not in the results seen.
flavor: Sweet-leaning kanro-type shoyu according to the brand name.
use: Shoyu for dipping and finishing.
craft: Process data absent from results; verify directly with the maker.

name: Kikuhime (Hakusan, Ishikawa)
text: Sake brewer in Hakusan, Ishikawa; sources give founding variously as Eiroku 13 (1570) or the Tensho era (1573-92) as 'Oyanagiya', with 1902 as an incorporation date. House rule: if you have to ask someone else to polish your rice, stop brewing, so all rice is polished in-house. In 1983 it released the first sake labelled 'yamahai-jikomi'. 'Tsuru no Sato' is a yamahai junmai, 65 percent polish, 16 percent alcohol, from Yamada Nishiki of the Tokku district of Yoshikawa, Miki.
flavor: Rich, full-bodied yamahai style with strong rice umami.
use: Limited annual release in early October; for rich foods.
craft: Yamahai starter, 65 percent polish; Tsuru no Sato won the first Champion Sake.

name: Seiun Shuzo (Ogawa, hana-kobo)
text: Sake brewery in Ogawa town, Saitama, founded 1902, using flower yeast (hana-kobo). It is one of three Ogawa breweries, all drawing on the town's clear streams.
use: Local sake of Ogawa.
craft: The flower yeast is the defining technical point.

name: Matsuoka Jozo (Teimatsu, Ogawa)
text: Ogawa town brewery whose brand is Teimatsu, running from 1851 in the Edo period, one of Ogawa's three remaining breweries along with Seiun Shuzo and Musashizuru Shuzo.
use: Regional sake from the Saitama west.
craft: Details beyond date and place not in results.

name: Matsumoto Shoyu Shoten (Kawagoe, Hatsukari)
text: Kawagoe soy sauce maker, billed as about 250 years old. Its kura was built in Tenpo 1 (1830) and it makes natural-brewed 'Hatsukari shoyu' with two-year saishikomi in cedar barrels.
use: Dipping, sashimi and finishing.
craft: Saishikomi means brewing with shoyu in place of brine; two years, cedar barrels, natural fermentation.

name: Busyu Men (Ogawa)
text: Noodle maker in Ogawa town, Saitama, over 100 years old, producing dried and fresh noodles and running its own udon and soba restaurant. It belongs to the Musashino udon area of west Saitama.
use: Dried and fresh noodles for udon and soba.
craft: Flour selected for quality; both dried and fresh lines.

name: Ozawa Shuzo (Sawanoi, Ome)
text: Sake brewery in Ome, Tokyo, founded in Genroku 15 (1702) in Musashi's Sawai village; the brand 'Sawanoi' is taken from the village name. Related shop 'Mamagotoya' makes tofu and yuba dishes.
use: Sake and tofu/yuba table.
craft: Founding from old documents; brand named for place.

name: Ishikawa Shuzo (Tamajiman, Fussa)
text: Sake brewery in Fussa, Tokyo, making 'Tamajiman', listed on the Tokyo brewers' list as founded in Bunkyu 3 (1863).
use: Regional sake.
craft: Details not in results.

name: Ninben (Nihonbashi)
text: Katsuobushi house at Nihonbashi Muromachi, Tokyo, founded Genroku 12 (1699), when the first owner began selling katsuobushi and dried fish at Yokkaichi, Nihonbashi. Honkarebushi, matured by repeated mold-ing and sun-drying, was established in late Edo to Meiji; most shaved bonito is arabushi (smoked-dried). In 1969 it developed 'Fresh Pack' shaved bonito, and left the process unpatented.
use: Dashi; shaved bonito.
craft: Honkarebushi means repeated mold inoculation and sun drying; arabushi is smoked.

name: Suzuhiro (Odawara kamaboko)
text: Odawara kamaboko maker, 1865 (Keio 1). The roots lie in a fish business from around 1780; in 1865 the fourth Muraya Gon'emon started making kamaboko.
use: Kamaboko for Odawara cuisine.
craft: Details not in results.

name: Shimizu Shuzo (Kanagawa)
text: Kanagawa brewery cited on the prefecture's page as founded Horeki 1 (1751). Kanagawa has 14 breweries.
use: Local sake.
craft: Only date given.

name: Aburaden Miso (Tochigi city)
text: Miso maker in Tochigi city, founded 1781, using a Meiji-era dozo and wooden tubs in use since the Meiji era to age additive-free miso naturally. Also brews craft beer.
use: Miso and miso ramen.
craft: Old wooden barrels, natural ageing.

name: Seo Koji-ten (Mashiko)
text: Koji and miso shop in Mashiko, Tochigi, saying it is 120 years old, additive-free and naturally brewed, boiling soybeans over wood fire.
use: Koji for miso.
craft: Wood-fired soybean boil.

name: Honda Koji-ya (Tochigi city)
text: Koji and miso shop in Tochigi city using only domestic soybean, rice, barley and natural salt.
use: Miso and koji.
craft: Four raw materials.

name: Aogen Miso (Utsunomiya)
text: Utsunomiya miso house advertised as 400 years old; one shinise list gives 1625. Offers hand-made miso making experiences.
use: Miso and workshop.
craft: 1625 not confirmed.
